title: ACT Reading — Practice Test 4
summary: A full timed enhanced-ACT Reading test: four original passages (a Delta village literary narrative, humanities on the scales of Arabic music, social science on Cairo's sabil-kuttab buildings and natural science on desert locusts with a data table), 36 questions in 40 minutes, with a reason for every answer choice.

blocks.text: This is a full-length practice test for the **Reading section of the enhanced ACT**: **36 questions in 40 minutes**, four passages with 9 questions each. In the real test, **27 questions are scored** and one passage is unscored, but you will not know which one, so treat every passage as if it counts. **In this practice test, all 36 questions count.** All passages and questions are original.

items: Sit in a quiet place, put your phone away and keep scrap paper and a pencil ready.
Do the whole section in one sitting. The timer starts when you press Start and the section ends automatically after 40 minutes.
Aim for about **10 minutes per passage**: roughly 3–4 minutes to read and map it, then about 6 minutes for its 9 questions.
For the passage with a table, read the title and column headings first; then answer table questions from the numbers, not from memory.
There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can, guess, mark it and move on.
The score shown at the end is a **practice percentage**, not an official ACT scaled score.

questions.p:
Passage I — Literary Narrative

LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is from an original short story. The narrator remembers a night from his boyhood in a village in the Nile Delta.

[1] In our village the canal water did not belong to anyone, which meant that everyone watched it. Each family's fields drew from the canal in turn, and the turns were set by an old agreement that no one had written down but everyone could recite: so many hours for the Sharkawis, so many for the widow Umm Hany, so many for us. That autumn our turn fell between midnight and dawn.

[2] My father usually took the night turns, but he was working in Alexandria that season, and my grandfather announced at supper that I would go with him. My mother objected that I had school in the morning. My grandfather replied that the school would still be there at eight o'clock and the water would not, and that was the end of the discussion.

[3] We set out a little before midnight, my grandfather carrying a hoe over his shoulder and I carrying a lantern I did not need, because the moon was almost full. The path along the canal was pale and hard. The frogs stopped singing as we came near and began again behind us, so that we seemed to walk inside a small moving pocket of silence. My grandfather did not talk. He walked the way he did everything, without hurry and without stopping.

[4] When we reached our land, the Sharkawis' pump was still running. Its engine coughed in the dark, and the water was still flowing into their field, not ours. I looked at my grandfather's watch, which he had let me wear for the night, and told him that their time had ended twenty minutes before. He nodded as though I had told him the weather.

[5] "Their rice is thirsty," he said. "Look at the far corner." I looked and saw nothing but darkness and the shine of water. "The land there is low," he said, "so the water runs to it first and stays. The high corner near the path is still dry. Old Sharkawi knows. He'll stop when the high corner drinks."

[6] I wanted to say that this was not our problem. I had been taught at school that rules exist so that people do not have to depend on kindness, and I said something like this, in the slightly superior tone I used that year for most things. My grandfather leaned on his hoe and considered it.

[7] "That is true," he said. "And the rules are why he will stop. But a rule is a fence, not a field. You still have to decide how to walk inside it."

[8] I did not know what to say to that, so I sat down on the canal bank and waited. The pump coughed on. At some point I must have fallen asleep, because the next thing I remember is the silence, and my grandfather's hand on my shoulder, and the sound of our own water running into our field through the gap he had opened in the earth wall with his hoe.

[9] We worked until the sky turned grey. He showed me how to close one channel and open another so that the water reached every row, and how to watch the surface: where it shone flat and still, the ground had drunk enough; where it crept forward in thin fingers, the land was higher and needed more time. "Water tells you where the land is low," he said. "People are the same, if you watch them."

[10] Walking home, I asked him whether he was angry about the twenty minutes. He seemed surprised by the question. He said that Old Sharkawi would remember them in the spring, when our wheat needed water and his did not, and that a debt like that was worth more than the water itself. Then he added, more quietly, that he had not done it for the debt.

[11] I went to school that morning with mud on my shoes and slept through most of a geography lesson about the irrigation of the Nile Delta. I failed the quiz that followed. I have always thought, though, that I learned more about the subject that night than the teacher could have expected.
questions.q: The passage mainly focuses on:
c: the narrator's poor results at school during his boyhood.
a bitter quarrel between two village families over the canal.
the father's work in Alexandria and why he left the village.
a night when the narrator helps his grandfather water their fields and learns something about how to treat neighbours.
questions.e: The story covers one night of irrigation and the lesson the grandfather teaches by waiting for his neighbour. B fails because no quarrel takes place.
ce: Too narrow: the failed quiz is a small, humorous detail at the very end.
Contradicted: the grandfather is calm, and there is no quarrel at all.
Off target: the father's work is mentioned only to explain why the narrator went instead.
Right: the night of irrigation and the grandfather's patience with the Sharkawis are the heart of the story.

Passage II — Humanities

HUMANITIES: This passage is from an original essay about the scales of Arabic music. The musician quoted is fictional.

[1] Play a melody in maqam Rast on a piano and something goes wrong. The tune is recognisable, but it sounds slightly flat in some places and slightly sharp in others, like a familiar face in a badly made photograph. The problem is not the pianist. It is the piano, which cannot play some of the notes that the melody needs.

[2] A piano divides the octave into twelve equal steps, and every melody played on it must use these twelve notes and no others. Arabic music, by contrast, is organised into maqamat (singular: maqam): melodic modes, each with its own set of notes, its own typical phrases and its own character. Several of the most important maqamat use notes that fall between the piano's keys. In Rast, for example, when the scale begins on the note C, the third note lies roughly halfway between the notes a pianist would call E-flat and E. Such notes are often called "quarter tones", because they seem to divide the piano's smallest step in half.

[3] The name is convenient but misleading. Musicians who play the oud or the violin do not find these notes by measuring; they place them by ear, and the exact position can vary from city to city, from maqam to maqam, and even from one phrase to the next. Many players say, for instance, that the half-flat E of maqam Bayati sits a little lower than the half-flat E of Rast. "We do not play quarter tones," says the oud player Adel Mansour. "We play the notes of the maqam. 'Quarter tone' is a name for people who need a ruler."

[4] For much of the twentieth century, these notes were at the centre of a debate about the future of Arabic music. In 1932, Cairo hosted a congress of Arab music that brought together musicians and scholars from across the Arab world and from Europe. One of the questions they discussed was the scale itself. Should Arabic music adopt a fixed system of notes so that it could be written down and taught in schools in a standard way? Or would fixing the notes destroy something essential?

[5] Those who favoured a fixed system had serious arguments. A standard scale would make it easier to write music down, and written music could be shared, studied and preserved. Many proposals described the octave as twenty-four equal quarter tones: the piano's twelve steps, each divided in two. The system was neat, and in later decades it appeared in many textbooks and music schools.

[6] Its critics, however, pointed out that it described the music only approximately. A melody written in twenty-four equal steps and played exactly as written would sound, to a trained ear, much like the Rast played on the piano: almost right, which is a particular kind of wrong. For these musicians, the living tradition was the true record of the scale, and any written system could only be a guide to it.

[7] In practice, both sides got part of what they wanted. Notation using signs for half-flat and half-sharp notes became common, and students today learn to read it. But teachers still insist that the page is only a starting point. A student learns the real positions of the notes the way students always have: by listening to masters and imitating them until the ear is satisfied. Instruments that let the player adjust every note, such as the fretless oud and the violin, remain at the heart of the music partly because they allow these fine differences.

[8] The debate has never been completely settled, and perhaps it cannot be. Every music that is written down faces the same problem in some form: a page holds less than a performance. What makes the Arabic case so clear is that the missing part can be heard. Play the piano's Rast and then the oud's Rast one after the other, and the difference is not a theory. It is a sound.

Passage III — Social Science

SOCIAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about the sabil-kuttab, a type of charitable building in historic Cairo. The historian quoted is fictional.

[1] In the old streets of Cairo, a visitor often meets a building that seems to do two jobs at once. At street level, behind tall windows covered with metal grilles, is a sabil, a public drinking fountain. Above it, under a wooden balcony open on several sides, is a kuttab, a small elementary school. This combination, known as a sabil-kuttab, appeared in Cairo in the Mamluk period and became especially common under the Ottomans, when many were built along the city's busiest roads.

[2] Water in a hot city was never a small matter. Before modern pipes, most of Cairo's drinking water came from the Nile, carried into the city in leather skins by water-carriers and their animals and sold by the load. For poor families, buying water every day was a real expense. A sabil offered it free. On hot days its window was one of the busiest spots on the street, as porters, traders and children stopped to drink. Beneath the building lay a large underground cistern, filled during the season of the Nile flood, when water was plentiful. An attendant drew water from it and handed it through the window grilles to anyone who asked.

[3] The school above served a different need. In a kuttab, young boys, often orphans or the children of poor families, learned to read and write and to memorise the Quran. Founders' documents frequently set out the details: the number of pupils, the teacher's salary, even the clothes the children were to receive each year at the feasts. "These were not vague promises," says the historian Laila Abdel-Fattah, who has studied many such documents. "A founder could specify how many pupils would be taught and what the teacher would earn, and the courts could enforce it."

[4] What made this possible was the waqf, a charitable endowment. A founder set aside property—shops, houses, farmland—whose income was dedicated permanently to a particular purpose. The rent from a row of shops might pay for the water to fill the cistern, the attendant's wages, the teacher's salary and the repair of the building. In principle, a waqf could keep a sabil-kuttab working long after its founder had died, and some continued for centuries.

[5] Why did wealthy Cairenes choose this particular form of charity? Religious motives were central: giving water to the thirsty was regarded as one of the most rewarded of good deeds, and teaching children was another. But Abdel-Fattah argues that the buildings also served their founders in more worldly ways. A sabil-kuttab stood on a public street, often at a corner where it could be seen from two directions, and its marble panels, carved inscriptions and painted woodwork displayed the founder's name and taste to every passer-by. "It was charity," she says, "but it was also a kind of signature on the city."

[6] One of the best-known examples, the sabil-kuttab of Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda, built in the eighteenth century, stands where a street divides in two in the heart of historic Cairo. Its position is no accident. Thirsty travellers on either branch of the street could see it, and so could anyone who wished to know which family had paid for it.

[7] In the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, piped water and state schools gradually took over both of the building's tasks. Many sabils fell silent, their cisterns dry, and many kuttabs closed. Some buildings were neglected, their carved woodwork slowly decaying in the dust; others were restored as monuments or turned into small museums and libraries.

[8] Abdel-Fattah sees in them a lesson that outlasts their original purpose. Long before modern governments provided water and schooling as public services, she points out, private individuals in Cairo had created institutions that offered both, free of charge, to anyone who walked by. "We tend to think of public services as a modern invention," she says. "The sabil-kuttab reminds us that people found other ways to meet the same needs."

Passage IV — Natural Science

NATURAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about how desert locusts change their behaviour. The research team and the data in the table are fictional.

[1] For most of its life, a desert locust is an unremarkable insect. Alone in the dry scrub of North Africa, the Middle East or South Asia, it is a shy, greenish grasshopper that avoids others of its kind and is easy to overlook. Yet under the right conditions the same species can form swarms that cover many square kilometres, contain millions upon millions of insects and eat almost every green thing in their path. The difference between the two lives is not a difference of species. It is a change that happens inside individual insects.

[2] Scientists call the two forms the solitarious phase and the gregarious phase. Solitarious locusts avoid one another; gregarious locusts are attracted to one another, are far more active and march or fly together. Over generations, gregarious locusts also come to look different: young ones develop bold black and yellow markings instead of green, and adults differ in body shape. But the first change—the switch in behaviour—can happen within hours.

[3] What triggers it is crowding. After good rains, plants spring up, locusts breed and their numbers grow. When the rain stops and the plants dry out, the insects are forced together onto the patches of green that remain. There, they bump into one another constantly. Researchers have long known that crowding causes the switch, but they wanted to know exactly which part of crowding mattered: the sight of other locusts, their smell or physical contact. All of these cues are present in a crowd, so simply watching crowded locusts could not tell them apart.

[4] A team led by the entomologist Rana Selim designed an experiment to separate these cues. Young solitarious locusts were exposed for four hours to different conditions, and then each was tested in a small arena with a group of other locusts behind a screen at one end. A locust that moved towards the group and stayed active was scored as behaving gregariously. Each condition was tested on a separate group of fifty insects, so no locust experienced more than one condition. The results appear in the table.

Condition (4 hours) | Locusts tested | Behaving gregariously
1. Kept alone (no cues) | 50 | 4
2. Sight and smell of other locusts, no touch | 50 | 15
3. Hind legs touched gently with a fine brush, no other locusts | 50 | 36
4. Crowded together with other locusts | 50 | 41

[5] The results pointed clearly to touch. Locusts that could see and smell others but never touch them changed much less than those whose hind legs were brushed, even though the brushed insects never met another locust at all. Selim's team concluded that repeated touching of the hind legs is the strongest single trigger, while sight and smell add a smaller effect. Crowding works best because in a crowd all of these cues arrive together.

1. Kept alone (no cues) | 50 | 4
2. Sight and smell of other locusts, no touch | 50 | 15

"We like to think an animal simply is what it is," Selim says. "The locust shows that sometimes an animal becomes what its situation makes it."
questions.q: Based on paragraph 7, monitoring programmes pay attention to rain in desert breeding areas mainly because:
c: heavy rain kills most young locusts.
rain followed by drying plants creates the conditions that can crowd locusts together and lead to swarms.
locusts are easier to see during rain.
rain stops locusts from producing serotonin.
questions.e: Rain lets numbers grow, and drying plants then crowd the insects, as paragraphs 3 and 7 explain. A invents an effect of rain not found in the passage.
ce: Not in the passage; rain is linked to breeding, not death.
Right: paragraph 7 names 'rain ... followed by drying vegetation' as the conditions that lead to swarms.
Not in the passage.
Not supported: rain and serotonin are never connected.

questions.q: Selim's statement that 'sometimes an animal becomes what its situation makes it' (paragraph 8) mainly serves to:
c: argue that genes have no effect on how animals behave.
express the broader lesson that one animal can develop very differently depending on what it experiences.
suggest that locusts deliberately choose to join swarms.
introduce a new experiment that the team plans to carry out.
questions.e: The closing quotation draws a general lesson about flexibility. A is too extreme for a passage that says 'the same genes' produce both forms.
ce: Too extreme: the passage says the same genes can produce both forms, not that genes do not matter.
